rules.sentence: Meckel’s diverticulitis is a result of obstruction to the neck of the diverticulum that can occur secondary to inflammatory narrowing, stricture formation, or mechanical obstruction due to enteroliths or other less common causes such as food, foreign body, or mass.

If identified on CT, it is seen as a blind-ended diverticulum in the distal small bowel away from the ileocecal junction, demonstrating wall thickening, increased wall enhancement, and surrounding mesenteric fat stranding with associated inflammatory changes in the adjacent segment of the small bowel (Fig. 14).
Meckel’s diverticulitis can be complicated by perforation, leading to localized or generalized pneumoperitoneum and secondary abscess formation (Fig. 14).

If an inflamed Meckel’s diverticulum is not identified on imaging, local inflammatory changes involving the bowel and mesentery can mimic other causes of bowel wall thickening described in the section on differential diagnoses of small bowel diverticulitis.
Careful assessment of axial, coronal, and sagittal CT images helps accurately identify Meckel’s diverticulum or diverticulitis.
Meckel’s diverticulum can mimic appendicitis or an appendiceal mucocele (Fig. 15).
